kaigo-eating-01-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Identify staple foods and side dishes on a menu and answer questions about the dishes.
Distinguish sensory recognition from digestion and swallowing.

kaigo-eating-01-knowledge-0.heading: The meaning of eating and the senses
paragraphs: Meals provide nutrition to sustain life and activity, while offering enjoyment and social connection. Eating by mouth also stimulates the brain and helps establish daily rhythms.

Eating uses several senses: seeing color and shape, noticing aroma, and experiencing taste and texture. Hand movements, chewing and swallowing follow too. Recognizing a dish alone does not establish overall eating ability.

kaigo-eating-01-knowledge-1.heading: The route of food, digestion and absorption
paragraphs: Food passes from the mouth through the esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. After digestion and absorption, the remainder becomes stool and leaves through the rectum and anus. In the mouth, food is chewed and mixed with saliva; stomach fluids and movement continue digestion.

Digestion breaks food down; absorption brings needed components into the body. Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine, while water is also absorbed in the large intestine. Distinguish digestive functions from bringing food to the mouth.

Bile made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder, and digestive fluids from the pancreas, also aid digestion. Distinguish the digestive tract that food passes through from organs supplying digestive fluids.

kaigo-eating-01-knowledge-2.heading: Distinguish the menu from the individual meal
paragraphs: Read the staple, side dishes and drinks for the relevant meal and day. A person saying the meal was delicious matters, but does not alone establish the amount eaten or adequate nutrition.
Dish names do not establish ingredients, allergies, texture or treatment-related restrictions. Both ask the person’s wishes and check that the meal matches the confirmed individual plan.

kaigo-eating-01-knowledge-3.heading: Receive information through sight and hearing
paragraphs: In the eye, the cornea and lens help focus light; the retina receives it and information travels through the optic nerve to the brain. When vision is difficult, check specific problems, such as reading text or recognizing dishes.

In the ear, the eardrum receives sound vibrations, the ossicles transmit them and the cochlea converts them into signals that reach the brain through the auditory nerve. Receiving and transmitting are different functions. Care workers do not diagnose the impairment’s location from symptoms alone; check suitable explanations.
The inner ear contains the hearing-related cochlea and vestibular structures involved in balance. Distinguish hearing from balance and report the actual difficulties.

kaigo-eating-02-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain chewing, swallowing, aspiration and choking as distinct concepts.
Check the person’s meal before serving rather than guessing an unreadable label.

kaigo-eating-02-knowledge-0.heading: Distinguish chewing, swallowing and aspiration
paragraphs: Eating includes recognizing food, chewing and mixing it with saliva into a bolus, moving it toward the throat with the tongue and other structures, passage through the pharynx, and movement through the esophagus to the stomach. Chewing and swallowing are different functions.

Eating and swallowing disorders involve difficulty in this process. Aspiration is food or saliva entering the airway below the vocal folds; choking is an obstruction that interferes with breathing. Do not diagnose from one sign or assume no problem because there is no coughing response.

kaigo-eating-02-knowledge-1.heading: Adapt food texture to each person
paragraphs: Softening, chopping, pureeing and adjusting liquid thickness must match chewing and swallowing abilities. Do not universally assume small pieces are safe or liquids are easy.

Before serving, verify the person, meal time, texture and confirmed ingredient, allergy and restriction information. If labels are unreadable or conflict with the plan, ask the person responsible. Do not compensate by independently chopping or adding thickener.

kaigo-eating-02-knowledge-2.heading: Limits when noticing a change
paragraphs: While providing trained support, care workers observe posture, eating, chewing and swallowing and report changes. Do not feed more to test a suspected problem.

For urgent signs such as breathing abnormalities, seek immediate help through facility emergency procedures. Do not independently give water to clear an obstruction. This text does not teach practical choking-rescue procedures.

kaigo-eating-02-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] At meal collection, the name on the label is Haruko Morikawa, but the texture information is blurred. Kitchen worker Miura cannot confirm the current texture either. Consult before serving and do not provide the tray until checks are complete.

kaigo-depth-16.heading: A texture name alone does not establish safety
paragraphs: Chopped food consists of small pieces that may scatter. Soft food is softened while retaining shape; pureed food is smooth. Consider both chewing and swallowing, including thickness adjustment. Small pieces or high water content alone do not establish safety.

Check the person, meal, planned texture, restrictions and allergies. Observe shape, softness, cohesion and fluid separation, but appearance does not replace individual swallowing assessment. Confirm discrepancies before serving.

Foods mixing solids and liquids may differ from foods of a uniform consistency. With low intake, consider the mouth, teeth, chewing and swallowing rather than preferences alone, and report observations. Do not independently add water, mash everything or change thickness.
This explains textures and why checks matter. Actual adjustments follow individual assessment and plans, product instructions, facility procedures and practical training.

kaigo-eating-03-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain stable posture and the purpose of adaptive utensils.
Preserve the person’s independent actions and adjust dish position within consent.

kaigo-eating-03-knowledge-0.heading: Why a stable posture matters
paragraphs: A suitable chair and table, stable body and supported soles help someone use their hands and eat independently. Alongside sitting back in the chair, check for unsupported feet, sliding or leaning through fatigue.

A raised chin can make swallowing harder. However, do not impose one head position or chin-tuck action on everyone; follow individual assessment and the plan. Check bed-based eating methods separately from chair-based eating.

kaigo-eating-03-knowledge-1.heading: Assistive utensils and what the person can do
paragraphs: Easy-grip handles, nonslip mats and easy-scoop plates compensate for particular difficulties. A useful appearance does not establish suitability. Check the planned equipment and how to use it.
Distinguish what the person can do from the help requested. Asking to bring a dish closer is not consent to moving their hand or feeding the entire meal.

kaigo-eating-03-knowledge-2.heading: Checks before starting
paragraphs: Check condition, appropriate posture, clean hands, meal contents and restrictions; explain and obtain consent. Also check that the food is positioned where the person can recognize it.

The helper chooses a height and position allowing observation and conversation. Approaching from high above or rushing food toward the mouth can make the person raise their face. Positioning, spoon handling and bed-based assistance require practical training.

kaigo-eating-03-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] In the dining room, Morikawa has not begun eating. They can use a spoon, but the dish is too far away. The plan permits repositioning the dish according to their wishes. This is not practice in supporting the hand or bringing food to the mouth.

kaigo-depth-14.heading: Posture and the care worker’s position during meals
paragraphs: Sitting back in a suitable chair with supported soles and a stable body also supports hand use. Check the table, body and helper’s position so the person need not extend their neck to look up. Head and chin positions follow individual assessment.

For bed-based eating, adjust back elevation and head and body support according to the plan, checking sliding and skin pressure. If raising the upper body is difficult, the source shows an example involving hemiplegia with the unaffected side down. It does not prescribe one direction for everyone.

Position the helper at a suitable height for eye contact and observation of expression and the mouth. Do not choose bed or chair solely for staff comfort; review unsupported feet, sliding pelvis and fatigue. A tidy posture does not replace checking condition, alertness and swallowing assessment.

Do not attempt unfamiliar positioning or assistance from this text alone. Specific angles, supports and suitability for side-lying depend on the person’s condition, individual plan and practical training.

kaigo-eating-04-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain food locations from the person’s perspective.
Make heat and unknowns clear and recheck temperature after waiting.

kaigo-eating-04-knowledge-0.heading: Describe food locations to a person with reduced vision
paragraphs: Ask what explanation is easiest to understand. For clock-position descriptions, agree on a clock from the person’s perspective, with twelve farthest away and six nearest. Do not confuse it with the worker’s left and right.
Clock descriptions do not suit everyone. Explain temperature and seasoning as well as location. Announce changes in arrangement; pointing alone does not prove the location was conveyed.

kaigo-eating-04-knowledge-1.heading: Information about hot and cold food
paragraphs: Temperature affects enjoyment, but safe serving still needs checking. Acknowledge when the person finds food hot; waiting a while does not guarantee safety based on time alone.

Waiting for cooling differs from adding water and changing consistency. Recheck temperature and do not independently change texture or drink instructions. Sensation and temperature regulation can be affected by health, so the person’s sensation alone does not establish every safety condition.

kaigo-eating-04-knowledge-2.heading: Give information in parts and check understanding
paragraphs: Use the preferred explanation, avoid giving too many positions and cautions at once, and check as needed. Repeating “Tofu at the back, rice on the right” can show the shared directional understanding.
Being able to locate food does not establish checked texture or allergies. Identify exactly what remains unknown rather than promising unconfirmed safety.

kaigo-depth-15.heading: Consider which action an assistive utensil supports
paragraphs: Easy-grip handles help holding, and angled spoons help adjust the direction toward the mouth. Spring-assisted chopsticks, spoon-holding straps, handled cups, easy-scoop plates and nonslip mats are also selected for particular difficulties.

Observe retained and difficult actions and ask about comfort with planned aids. Check size, position and cleanliness, then review whether an adjustment makes independent eating easier. Availability alone does not establish suitable support.

Do not choose the same equipment set from diagnosis alone. An easy-grip cup does not permit freely changing drinking speed, liquid consistency or straw suitability. Check for tight straps, skin pain and similar problems too.
Adaptive aids help specific movements; they do not automatically resolve swallowing disorders. Actual use follows individual assessment and plans, equipment instructions and facility training.

kaigo-eating-05-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain why eating observations and a suitable pace matter.
Distinguish a pause from finishing, and report the person’s wishes and condition.

kaigo-eating-05-knowledge-0.heading: Support eating at the person’s pace
paragraphs: Distinguish independent eating, partial help and assistance bringing food to the mouth. Do not increase help for staff convenience; match mouthful size and pace to the person’s condition and plan.
Observe whether the previous mouthful has been swallowed and whether food remains. Do not add food continuously. Avoid talking to the person while they chew; choose a time when they can speak.

kaigo-eating-05-knowledge-1.heading: Observation and consultation during meals
paragraphs: Observe posture, pace, hand and mouth movements, chewing and swallowing. Describe coughing responses, repeated coughs, voice changes, breathlessness, fatigue or discomfort specifically.

Do not diagnose from one sign or use absence of coughing as proof of no aspiration. Do not continue unsuitable assistance; follow facility procedures for help or professional checks. Do not prioritize lengthy questions in an emergency.

kaigo-eating-05-knowledge-2.heading: Ask whether the person wants to finish or take a break
paragraphs: If the person wants rest or no more food, do not blame leftovers or force the target amount. Check whether they want a pause or to finish; consider resuming only after checking wishes and condition.
After the meal, confirm completion, remaining food in the mouth, oral care and resting posture according to the plan. Uniform fluid amounts or rest periods do not replace individual assessment.

kaigo-eating-05-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Hasebe has stopped eating and has no food in the mouth when requesting rest. The cause is unknown. The worker acknowledges the wish and reports eating observations through facility procedures. This is not questioning during chewing.

kaigo-depth-17.heading: Connect care before, during and after meals
paragraphs: Before eating, check condition, identity, meal contents and texture, restrictions, allergies and posture. Explain and obtain consent, clean the hands and describe the menu. During eating, follow suitable mouthful sizes and pace and check swallowing.

Sit where the person need not extend the neck. Handle the spoon without making them lift the head; the source describes withdrawing it horizontally. The hemiplegia example of assisting at the unaffected corner of the mouth also requires individual planning and training. Do not add another mouthful while food remains; avoid talking during chewing and wait until the person can speak.

The source gives tea or soup before eating as an example of moistening the mouth. However, drink type, consistency and whether it may be taken depend on the plan. Do not prescribe thin tea for everyone or give it as a response to coughing during eating.

Confirm with the person that eating is finished, check food remaining in the mouth and arrange oral care. The source’s roughly thirty minutes seated after a meal is a learning reference; individual positioning and rest follow assessment and planning. Understand why immediately lying down is not automatically appropriate.

If coughing, voice changes, breathlessness, fatigue or oral residue appears, do not force continued eating; seek suitable help or checks. No cough alone does not establish safety. Record known food and fluid intake, the person’s words and support provided.

kaigo-eating-06-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Distinguish amount eaten, amount left and unconfirmed information.
Separate observations from the person’s words and report to the nurse without assuming causes.

kaigo-eating-06-knowledge-0.heading: Clearly distinguish amounts eaten and left
paragraphs: Records specify whose meal, which meal, the time and amounts for each dish, identifying eaten versus remaining amounts. Distinguish visual estimates from measured values and use consistent units.

Unconfirmed does not mean zero. Distinguishing statements, observations and unknowns such as causes helps the team follow events. One meal’s intake does not establish adequate nutrition or illness as the cause.

kaigo-eating-06-knowledge-1.heading: Endocrine function and meal information
paragraphs: Endocrine organs release hormones regulating many functions. The pancreas is one, and insulin helps regulate blood glucose. Learning physiology differs from diagnosing an individual.

Diabetes concerns glucose regulation, but low intake alone does not establish it as the cause. Care workers do not change medication or prescribed meal times based on assumptions; report observations.

kaigo-eating-06-knowledge-2.heading: Immunity and everyday health
paragraphs: Immunity is the response protecting the body from pathogens such as bacteria and viruses. Lifestyle and mental and physical condition affect it. Balanced food and rest help support health.
Eating one particular dish does not guarantee freedom from infection. Distinguish nutritional support from infection prevention and continue both condition observations and standard precautions.

kaigo-eating-07-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain the body functions supporting eating and the reasons for assistance.
Explain differences between the common menu and individual plan, and repeat responsibilities for checks and communication.

kaigo-eating-07-knowledge-0.heading: The heart and two circulatory routes
paragraphs: The heart has four chambers: left and right atria and ventricles. It pumps through repeated contraction and relaxation. Systemic circulation carries oxygen and nutrients throughout the body; pulmonary circulation involves gas exchange as blood travels from the heart through the lungs and back.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it. Pulmonary arteries bring blood to the lungs before gas exchange; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood. Do not memorize only that arteries always contain more oxygen.

kaigo-eating-07-knowledge-1.heading: Bring together the functions that support eating
paragraphs: Eating combines sensory recognition, hand and mouth movements, chewing, swallowing, breathing and digestion. One successful action does not remove the need to check other functions.

Common menus and individual plans differ in scope and purpose. If they conflict, check the person, meal and current information. Avoid independently deciding from either sheet alone so the meal suits the person.

kaigo-eating-07-knowledge-2.heading: Explain your reasons and review the week
paragraphs: Explain posture through stability and swallowing, adaptive aids through difficult actions, and texture through chewing and swallowing abilities. Go beyond “ask the person responsible” to say what is known and unknown.
Respect choice and pace and help only where needed according to the plan. Separate actual intake from the person’s words. Review eaten, remaining and unknown amounts without confusing them.

kaigo-eating-07-words.heading: Vocabulary and expression reference
paragraphs: This list is a reference when needed, not a task to learn everything anew in one day. Check expressions for today’s conversation and review familiar terms as needed.
確認（かくにん） — Checking: asking or investigating uncertainty to establish reliable information.
記録（きろく） — Recording observations, statements and completed actions separately.
支援計画（しえんけいかく） — Support plan: planned assistance based on the person’s goals and condition.
未確認（みかくにん） — Unconfirmed: information not yet checked. It does not mean nothing is present.
食欲（しょくよく） — Appetite: the desire to eat.
献立（こんだて） — Menu: the combination of dishes provided for a meal.
主食（しゅしょく） — Staple food: a grain-based main component such as rice or bread.
副食（ふくしょく） — Side dishes eaten with the staple.
食品（しょくひん） — Food products used for eating or drinking.
食事形態（しょくじけいたい） — Food texture and form adjusted to chewing and swallowing abilities.
アレルギー（アレルギー） — Allergy: an excessive immune response to a specific substance, distinct from a preference.
嚥下（えんげ） — Swallowing: moving material from the mouth through the throat toward the esophagus.
誤嚥（ごえん） — Aspiration: food, drink or saliva entering the airway below the vocal folds.
とろみ（とろみ） — Thickness or viscosity of a liquid. The term is not permission for a care worker to change it freely.
こぼす（こぼす） — To spill food or liquid outside a container.
量（りょう） — Amount: how much there is. Specify whether it is eaten or left over.
冷ます（さます） — To cool something hot.
温める（あたためる） — To warm something by raising its temperature.
エプロン（えぷろん） — Apron: worn to protect clothing or similar surfaces from soiling.
きざむ（きざむ） — To chop food or other material finely.
下げる（さげる） — In “clear the dishes,” this means removing used tableware.
水分補給（すいぶんほきゅう） — Replacing the fluids the body needs. Follow the person’s plan for how and how much to drink.
咳込む（せきこむ） — To cough repeatedly.
粉（こな） — Powder: fine particles. As a standalone word it is generally read kona. In the course expression とろみ（粉）, the reading ko is supplied for 粉, referring to powder used to adjust thickness.
つける（つける） — In “add thickness,” this means making a liquid more viscous.
飲み込む（のみこむ） — To swallow: moving material from the mouth through the throat into the esophagus.
一口大（ひとくちだい） — Bite-sized: small enough to fit in the mouth in one bite. It does not define the same suitable amount for everyone.
むせる（むせる） — A coughing response during eating or similar situations. This alone does not establish whether aspiration occurred.
リーダー（りーだー） — Team leader: the person coordinating the team’s work.
あげもの（あげもの） — Deep-fried dishes.
いためもの（いためもの） — Stir-fried dishes: ingredients heated while moved in a small amount of oil.
おやつ（おやつ） — A snack between main meals, or snack time.
粥（かゆ） — Rice porridge or a similar grain cooked in plenty of water. Its name alone does not establish suitability for swallowing.
お粥（おかゆ） — Polite form of 粥, meaning rice porridge.
カレーライス（かれーらいす） — Curry rice: rice served with curry beside or over it.
献立表（こんだてひょう） — A chart listing dishes for each meal.
汁物（しるもの） — Soup or another dish containing broth, such as miso soup.
ゼリー（ぜりー） — Gel dessert: a food made by setting a liquid. The name alone does not establish swallowing suitability.
たまご焼き（たまごやき） — A dish made by beating and cooking eggs.
漬物（つけもの） — Pickles: vegetables or other ingredients preserved in salt or seasoned liquid.
天ぷら（てんぷら） — Tempura: ingredients coated in batter and deep-fried.
豆腐（とうふ） — Tofu: a soybean food made by setting soy milk.
丼（どんぶり） — A large, deep bowl, or a dish of rice topped with ingredients in such a bowl. Use context to distinguish the meanings.
煮付け（につけ） — Simmering ingredients in seasoned liquid to absorb flavor, or a dish prepared this way.
煮物（にもの） — A dish simmered with liquid and seasonings.
ハンバーグ（はんばーぐ） — Hamburger steak: ground meat and other ingredients shaped and cooked.
プリン（ぷりん） — A set dessert such as custard made with eggs and milk. Check ingredients for each product.
麦茶（むぎちゃ） — Barley tea: a drink made from barley.
メニュー（めにゅー） — A list of dishes offered; may refer to the meal plan.
焼き魚（やきざかな） — Grilled fish.
ヨーグルト（よーぐると） — Yogurt: a food made by fermenting milk or similar ingredients.

kaigo-eating-07-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Before dinner, Onodera’s common menu says rice, while the individual plan says porridge. The current plan is unconfirmed and the tray uncollected. Report the difference to Kawase and agree responsibilities instead of assuming which is correct.

Naoto Kawase: I haven’t checked the latest plan either. Have you collected the tray?

Care worker: You’ll check the plan, Kawase, and I’ll tell the kitchen the result. I’ll also compare the confirmed restriction and allergy information.

kaigo-eating-07-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply your learning to another situation

A substitute alone does not establish milk allergy. Do not alter dishes or claim collection before checking; seek clarification before serving.

kaigo-eating-02.title: Chewing, swallowing and food texture
objectives: Explain chewing, swallowing, aspiration and choking as distinct concepts.

kaigo-eating-02.context: [Situation created for learning] At meal collection, the name on the label is Haruko Morikawa, but the texture information is blurred. kaigo-eating-02.artCaption: If the food texture is unclear, check before serving, even if you can read the name.

kaigo-eating-03.title: Posture and surroundings for eating independently
objectives: Explain stable posture and the purpose of adaptive utensils.
Preserve the person’s independent actions and adjust dish position within consent.
kaigo-eating-03.context: [Situation created for learning] In the dining room, Morikawa has not begun eating. They can use a spoon, but the dish is too far away. kaigo-eating-04.title: Clearly describe food locations and temperature
objectives: Explain food locations from the person’s perspective.

kaigo-eating-04.context: [Situation created for learning] In this particular scenario, Onodera has visual difficulty and wants to know the arrangement before eating. kaigo-eating-04.artCaption: Describe food locations from the person’s viewpoint and also explain the temperature in words.

kaigo-eating-05.title: Respect the person’s eating pace and wish to rest
objectives: Explain why eating observations and a suitable pace matter.
Distinguish a pause from finishing, and report the person’s wishes and condition.
kaigo-eating-05.context: [Situation created for learning] Hasebe has stopped eating and has no food in the mouth when requesting rest. The cause is unknown. The worker acknowledges the wish and reports eating observations through facility procedures. This is not questioning during chewing.
kaigo-eating-05.artCaption: Acknowledge the wish to rest. Consider restarting the meal after checking the person’s wishes and condition.

kaigo-eating-06.title: Accurately record and report food intake
objectives: Distinguish amount eaten, amount left and unconfirmed information.
Separate observations from the person’s words and report to the nurse without assuming causes.
kaigo-eating-06.context: [Situation created for learning] Reporting privately to a nurse, the worker confirms at 12:35 p.m. that Haruko Morikawa ate about half the rice and a quarter of the side dishes. The person says they want no more. The reason and drink amount remain unknown; this is not an emergency scenario.
